items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 + dsv4 + DSPARK + HiCache: long agentic sessions get #cached-token: 0 every turn despite stable 50%+ prefix (short requests hit ~98%)
items.body:
# [Bug] DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 (dsv4 + DSPARK + HiCache): long agentic sessions get `#cached-token: 0` on every turn despite stable 50%+ token-level prefix, while short requests hit ~98%

## Summary

On a production deployment of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 (8×H20, TP=8, `dsv4` attention backend, DSPARK speculative decoding, HiCache `write_through_selective`), **long multi-turn agent sessions (Claude Code) get zero prefix-cache hits on every turn**, while short requests served in the same window hit ~98%. Token-weighted prefix hit rate over 5 hours of real traffic is **83.8%**, dominated by these large-request misses.

We verified on the **client side via packet capture** that the requests themselves are not at fault, so the root cause appears to be in the DSV4 hybrid-pool radix reuse path on the server.

## Environment

- sglang **v0.5.17** (image `lmsysorg/sglang:latest-cu130` built 2026-08-08, torch 2.11.0+cu130)
- 8 × NVIDIA H20-3e (SM90, 143.8 GB each), single node
- Model: `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` (`DeepseekV4ForCausalLM`, bundled DSpark draft head), TP=8
- Relevant server args:
  - `attention_backend='dsv4'`, `kv_cache_dtype='fp8_e4m3'`, `page_size=256` (auto-forced)
  - `swa_full_tokens_ratio=0.1`
  - `speculative_algorithm='DSPARK'`, `speculative_num_draft_tokens=6`
  - `enable_hierarchical_cache=True`, `hicache_ratio=1.0`, `hicache_write_policy='write_through_selective'`
  - `mem_fraction_static=0.69`, `chunked_prefill_size=32768`, `max_running_requests=8`
  - `schedule_policy='lpm'`, `radix_eviction_policy='lru'`
- Pool sizes at startup (per rank): `full=8,460,800, swa=846,080, c4=2,115,200, c128=66,100` (`DSV4 memory calculation: bytes_per_full_token=9259.90, available_bytes=73.17 GB`)
- Traffic: Claude Code native Anthropic protocol (`/v1/messages?beta=true` with `claude-code-20250219, interleaved-thinking, context-management, prompt-caching-scope` betas), relayed unchanged by a gateway; 6–13万-token prompts, 15–60 s per turn.

## Observed behavior

1. **Large sessions always miss.** A user session at ~110K prompt tokens issues consecutive turns 10–40 s apart, each turn a strict append of the previous turn (+100–2,000 tokens). Every turn logs chunked prefill as:
   ```
   Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 32768, #cached-token: 0
   Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 32768, #cached-token: 0
   Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 13568, #cached-token: 0
   ```
   Even the tail chunk of the same request only picks up leftovers from *other* users' sessions.

2. **Short requests in the same seconds hit fine** (`#new-token: 512, #cached-token: 80640`; `#new-token: 256, #cached-token: 212480`) — so the radix tree itself is functional.

3. **Eviction paradox.** Over ~5 h: `evicted_tokens_total = 9.08e8` (31,512 evictions, 271 s cumulative) vs `uncached_prompt_tokens = 6.37e7` — evicted tokens are **14× the uncached input** — yet peak `full token usage` is only **0.08** and the pool holds 8.46M tokens. Nothing is ever "full"; enormous churn happens anyway.

4. **HiCache load-back is ~dead**: `load_back_tokens_total = 14,336` over 5 hours, although `write_through_selective` writes the C4/C128 sidecars to host (SWA 21.28 GB + C4 25.99 GB + C128 1.14 GB host pools allocated per rank).

## Client-side verification (packet capture)

We tcpdump'ed the ingress and reassembled 17 complete consecutive JSON bodies from a single keep-alive connection (one Claude Code session). Findings:

- Adjacent turns share a **70–75% byte-level common prefix** (each turn = previous turn + appended messages; the drop from 100% is explained below).
- `tools` (23 entries) are **identical in name and order** across turns.
- The byte-level divergence point is exactly where Anthropic's `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` breakpoint **moves with the last user message** (positions: turn N → `messages[14]`, turn N+1 → `messages[16]`). The `system` blocks keep their two breakpoints at fixed positions.
- After stripping `cache_control` fields, the first 14 messages serialize **byte-identical** across turns (138,156 bytes = **53% of the full body**), i.e. a stable, reusable token prefix of well over 50% exists on every turn.

So the client presents a stable 50%+ prefix every 10–40 s, yet the server reports `#cached-token: 0` for the entire request. This rules out prompt drift / unstable tool ordering as the cause.

## Suspected area

Given short-prefix hits work and long-prefix (multi-chunk, 32K×n) reuse always fails, this looks like the DSV4 hybrid-group reuse/translation path — possibly the same family as:

- #33656 — deterministic SWA KV position corruption on the cached-prefix **restore** path under HiCache + high reuse (same model, same 8×H20 topology, same ~86% radix hit workload). Our deployment shows the same near-zero `load_back` on that path.
- #33549 — same model/hardware/software combo (8×H20 + Flash-0731 + dsv4 + DSPARK) hang at ~245K context.
- #26427 — HiSparse long-context concurrency issues traced to full-token→compressed-C4 location translation.
- vllm-project/vllm#42948 (upstream sibling engine) — DSv4-Flash hybrid groups losing first-block cache keys on every physical-block reassignment, cascading `hit_length` to 0 across all groups **while pool usage stays <10%** — which matches our eviction paradox (usage 8%, churn 14×) and the long-request-only miss pattern (long requests trigger many block allocations via chunked prefill; short requests don't).

## Reproduction

Replaying the two captured bodies back-to-back against the same server (turn 1 to warm the cache, turn 2 immediately after) reproduces `#cached-token: 0` for turn 2. Minimal data: any two Anthropic-protocol requests where request 2 = request 1 + 2 appended messages and prompt > ~64K tokens (i.e. ≥ 3 chunked-prefill chunks), sent within seconds of each other.

Happy to provide the captured request bodies (sanitized) and full startup logs if useful.

## Questions

1. Is long-prefix (multi-chunk) reuse expected to work with `write_through_selective` on v0.5.17, or is there a known regression fixed after v0.5.17 (we saw SWA-eviction-related fixes like #35809 and UnifiedRadixTree cache-hit-reset PRs #30468/#30636/#30626/#31643 land later)?
2. Could disabling `--enable-hierarchical-cache` restore correct long-prefix reuse as a temporary mitigation, at the cost of losing host-tier offload?

items.title: [Bug] apply_rotary_emb_flat_kernel rotates and overwrites the columns past rope_dim
items.body:
## Describe the bug

`apply_rotary_emb_triton` in `python/sglang/kernels/ops/attention/deepseek_v4_rope.py` picks one of three kernels for the same operation. Two of them mask the column axis against the real rotary width:

```python
apply_rotary_emb_triton_kernel          mask = offs_pair < (rope_dim // 2)      # :102
apply_rotary_emb_triton_kernel_batched  pair_mask = pair < (rope_dim // 2)      # :154
```

The third does not. `apply_rotary_emb_flat_kernel` is launched with `RD = max(triton.next_power_of_2(rope_dim), 2)` (:290) and walks `d = tl.arange(0, RD)`, but its load and its store carry only the *row* mask:

```python
d = tl.arange(0, RD)
xo = base + d[None, :] * sx_d
x = tl.load(x_ptr + xo, mask=rmask[:, None], other=0.0).to(tl.float32)   # :225
...
tl.store(x_ptr + xo, out.to(x_ptr.dtype.element_ty), mask=rmask[:, None])  # :254
```

The `cos` / `sin` loads at :232 and :237 have the same shape. So whenever `rope_dim` is not a power of two, the columns from `rope_dim` to `RD - 1` are read, rotated and written back. The kernel works in place, so those writes land on the next head's data — and on the final row, past the end of the tensor.

Both effects are visible:

- **Wrong values.** Against the library's own per-token kernel, selected by the same public call, `batch=4 n_heads=8 rope_dim=6` gives `max|flat - per_token| = 3.81` with 48 of 192 elements differing. `rope_dim` 96 and 192 happen to come out equal in that comparison, because each stray write lands inside the *next* head's region, where that head's own program writes the correct value too — but see below, they are still out of bounds.
- **Out-of-bounds access.** Under `compute-sanitizer`, `rope_dim=6` reads 5 bytes past the 96-byte `freqs` allocation at `:238`, and `rope_dim=96` reads 1 byte past the 12288-byte `x` allocation at `:225`. Both then die with `CUDA error: unspecified launch failure`.

**This is latent on the shipped configurations**, and the caveat belongs with the report: DeepSeek-V4 uses a power-of-two `rope_dim`, and the flat path is opt-in (`_USE_BATCHED_ROPE` is `False` by default, set by `set_batched_rope(True)` / `SGLANG_ROPE_BATCHED=1`). Nothing in the tree reaches it today. It is filed because the kernel silently disagrees with its two siblings over a parameter it already receives, so the first non-power-of-two rotary width to use this path gets wrong numbers rather than an error.

## Reproduction

```python
import torch, triton
from sglang.kernels.ops.attention.deepseek_v4_rope import (
    apply_rotary_emb_triton, precompute_freqs_cis, set_batched_rope)

batch, n_heads, rope_dim = 4, 8, 6          # RD = next_power_of_2(6) = 8
torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.randn(batch, n_heads, rope_dim, device="cuda")
freqs = precompute_freqs_cis(rope_dim, batch, 0, 10000.0, 1.0, 32, 1).to("cuda")

set_batched_rope(False)                      # per-token kernel: masks the columns
ref = apply_rotary_emb_triton(x.clone(), freqs)
set_batched_rope(True)                       # flat kernel: does not
got = apply_rotary_emb_triton(x.clone(), freqs)

print("max|flat - per_token|:", (got - ref).abs().max().item())
print("differing cells:", int((got - ref).abs().gt(1e-4).sum()), "of", got.numel())
```

```
max|flat - per_token|: 3.8119478225708008
differing cells: 48 of 192
```

And under the sanitizer, with `x` allocated last so the overrun reaches unallocated memory:

```
$ PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1 compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck python repro_oob.py 96

rope_dim=96 RD=128 stray columns=32; x is 3072 elements = 12288 bytes
========= Invalid __global__ read of size 16 bytes
=========     at apply_rotary_emb_flat_kernel+0x2df0 in deepseek_v4_rope.py:225
=========     by thread (24,0,0) in block (1,0,0)
=========     Access to 0x7f7faa403600 is out of bounds
=========     and is 1 bytes after the nearest allocation at 0x7f7faa400600 of size 12288 bytes
========= ERROR SUMMARY: 12 errors
```

## Expected behavior

The padded columns are neither read past the tensors nor written back, as in the two sibling kernels. `_fused_norm_rope_kernel` in the same file already carries the real width as a `ROPE_DIM: tl.constexpr` (:410) and masks with it (:438).

## Environment

- `sgl-project/sglang` at `92b1d382c`
- NVIDIA B200 (sm_100), driver 595.71.05
- torch 2.13.0+cu130, triton 3.7.1, Python 3.12

### Describe the bug

    self._data[layer_idx, :].scatter_add_(
RuntimeError: Index tensor must have the same number of dimensions as self tensor
Exception: Capture cuda graph failed: Index tensor must have the same number of dimensions as self tensor
```

**Root cause analysis:**

- `--enable-eplb` force-activates the expert distribution recorder (mode `stat`) — there is no way to disable it while EPLB is on.
- During CUDA graph capture of the DSPARK draft model, the draft's MoE forward path (`deepseek_v4_dspark.py` → `deepseek_v2.py forward_normal_dual_stream` → `select_experts`) reaches `on_select_experts` without a `with_current_layer` context, so `layer_idx` is `None`.
- `self._data[None, :]` adds a singleton dimension (becomes 2-D), and `scatter_add_(dim=0, index=..., src=...)` gets a 1-D index → dimension mismatch → RuntimeError inside graph capture → capture fails → scheduler exits → crash loop.

This is the same failure mode documented in #25355 for the MegaMoE path (`forward_mega_moe` unwrapped by `with_current_layer`, hook fires with `layer_idx=None`, identical error text), but reached through the **DSPARK draft worker** entry instead of the MegaMoE dispatch path. Verified the `expert_distribution.py` guard is still absent on main as of 2026-08-16.

Related prior art on spec-decode × EPLB/recorder incompatibility: #32105 / #32106 (EAGLE + expert-distribution-metrics during draft capture), #34846 (DSpark draft MoE skips expert-location dispatch under EPLB — correctness, acceptance 1.61→3.38 after fix), and the historical Qwen3 MTP+EPLB fixes #16044 / #19812 / #19232.

**Workaround:** disable EPLB (keep DSPARK). EPLB cannot be kept because `--expert-distribution-recorder-mode null` is rejected by arg validation (YAML null → string `"None"`, `invalid choice`), and EPLB force-enables the recorder anyway.

Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash (single checkpoint, DSpark head bundled), 8x H20-3e (141 GB, CC 9.0), TP=8 / EP=8.

enable-eplb: true          # <- toggling this line is the entire repro

2. Comment out `enable-eplb` + `ep-num-redundant-experts` → server starts and serves normally (verified, stable).

items.title: [Bug] DSPARK silently corrupts identifiers on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, making speculative decoding unsafe
items.body:
### Checklist - [x] I searched related issues but found no solution. - [x] The bug persists in the latest version. - [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback. - [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Describe the bug

Summary

On DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, SGLang’s DSPARK speculative decoding silently introduces single-character corruptions into identifiers supplied verbatim in the prompt:

kimi-k3   → kimi-kw
nova-x7   → nova-7
apollo-n9 → apollo-n11

The same server, weights, prompts, and launch configuration—with only speculative decoding disabled—produces zero such corruptions across thousands of grounded identifier tokens.

The corruption rate increases with the DSPARK verify-window width:

--speculative-dspark-block-size | speculative_num_draft_tokens | Temp 0 | Temp 1 -- | -- | -- | -- 6 | 7 | 1.03% | 0.82% 5 | 6 | 0.32% | 0.77% 1 | 2 | 0.00% | 0.00% Speculation disabled | — | 0.00% | 0.00%

Aggregated across both block_size=1 runs:

  • Temperature 0: 0 / 4561
  • Temperature 1: 0 / 3701

Using the rule of three, the corresponding approximate 95% upper bounds are:

  • Temperature 0: <0.066%
  • Temperature 1: <0.081%

This contrasts with the 1.03% observed rate at block_size=6, temperature 0.

Examples of corrupted identifiers

Malformed forms observed at block_size=6, temperature 0:

kimi-kw    -> kimi-k3   (x5)
kimi-k2    -> kimi-k3   (x3)
kimi-k7    -> kimi-k3   (x2)
apollo-n11 -> apollo-n9 (x2)
nova-12    -> nova-x7   (x2)
wq-7f2e    -> wq-7f2b   (x2)

kimi-kw2   -> kimi-k3
kimi-v2    -> kimi-k3
kimi-k11   -> kimi-k3
apollo-n12 -> apollo-n9
nova-7     -> nova-x7
nova-v7    -> nova-x7
wq-7f2e2   -> wq-7f2b

These are not malformed responses or obvious decoding failures. They are plausible-looking, single-character-wrong identifiers embedded in otherwise normal output.

Expected behavior

At temperature 0, DSPARK should emit the same greedy token sequence as the target model without speculative decoding.

A draft token should only be committed if it matches the corresponding target prediction. On mismatch, DSPARK should emit the target prediction instead.

Therefore, enabling DSPARK should not change grounded identifiers from:

kimi-k3

to:

kimi-kw

when the non-speculative target forward selects the correct token.

Actual behavior

With multi-position DSPARK verification enabled:

  • Grounded identifiers are silently corrupted.
  • The issue reproduces at temperature 0.
  • The issue requires or is strongly amplified by heterogeneous concurrent batching.
  • The rate increases with verify-window width.
  • No request error or warning is produced.
  • The finish reason remains normal.
  • Disabling speculation eliminates the corruption.
  • Reducing DSPARK to block_size=1 eliminates the corruption.

Hypotheses investigated and ruled out

1. Lossy accept/verify rule

This does not appear to be the cause.

Both accept_greedy and accept_greedy_triton in:

sglang/kernels/ops/speculative/dspark/dspark_accept.py

delegate to compute_dflash_correct_drafts_and_bonus in:

sglang/srt/speculative/dflash_utils.py

The relevant logic is:

matches = candidates[:, 1:] == target_predict[:, :-1]
correct_len = matches.to(torch.int32).cumprod(dim=1).sum(dim=1)
bonus = target_predict[torch.arange(bs, ...), correct_len]

Every committed token should therefore be either:

  1. An accepted draft token that compared equal to target_predict; or
  2. The bonus token, which is taken directly from target_predict.

A mismatching draft token should not be able to leak into the output.

This implies that the corrupted emitted tokens are likely themselves present in target_predict. In other words, the target verify forward appears to be producing incorrect logits or incorrect token alignment.

2. Ragged verify-window misalignment

accept_greedy performs:

torch.argmax(target_logits, dim=-1).view(
    bs, verify_num_draft_tokens
)

A dense reshape could misalign tokens if requests had different verify lengths.

However, SGLANG_RAGGED_VERIFY_MODE defaults to static. In static mode, resolve_ragged_verify_layout returns None, and verify lengths are uniform.

Therefore, the rectangular reshape is expected to be valid for this reproduction.

3. Numerical noise or batch-shape-dependent reductions

We tested three separate interventions. Each was verified to engage, and none removed the corruption.

FP32 LM head

Enabled:

--enable-fp32-lm-head

Engagement was confirmed empirically:

  • Before the change, 65.5% of recorded margins fell on the 0.25 BF16 grid.
  • After the change, 0% did.
  • There were zero exact ties across 34,420 records.

The typo rate did not improve.

Deterministic FP32 MoE reduction

We forced:

use_atomic_add = False

so the already-passed:

use_fp32_reduce = True

would engage.

In:

sglang/kernels/ops/moe/moe_wna16_marlin.py

the FP32 temporary buffer is allocated only under:

if use_fp32_reduce and not use_atomic_add:

This provides a structural confirmation that the path was active.

The observed rates remained approximately:

  • Temperature 0: 1.03%
  • Temperature 1: 0.82%

Tie epsilon on sampled accept path

Adding a tie epsilon to the sampled acceptance path had no effect.

More generally, an identifier repeated verbatim several times in the prompt should usually be a high-margin prediction. Low-order numerical noise would not be expected to repeatedly transform such identifiers into plausible alternatives.

The non-speculative control also varies in free-form prose between temperature-0 runs—likely due to prefix-cache or chunked-prefill effects—but it never corrupts a grounded identifier.

4. Draft/target gamma mismatch

The CLI can override the draft checkpoint’s declared gamma with only a warning:

DSpark gamma mismatch: using gamma=6
(from speculative_num_draft_tokens=7)
but draft config block_size=5.

This occurs in:

sglang/srt/speculative/dspark_components/dspark_config.py

The draft module itself obtains gamma from the checkpoint:

self.gamma = int(dspark_config.resolve_gamma(...))

in:

sglang/srt/models/deepseek_v4_dspark.py

This means the draft module and worker may disagree about the verify-window width.

However, running with block_size=5:

  • Makes the configured values agree
  • Removes the warning
  • Still reproduces the bug

Observed rates at block_size=5 were:

  • Temperature 0: 0.32%
  • Temperature 1: 0.77%

Therefore, the gamma mismatch is not the root cause of this corruption, although the silent override may be worth hardening as a separate issue.

5. Draft-side kernels

SGLANG_DSPARK_FAST_KERNEL only gates the draft forward.

Under a correct speculative verification rule, draft quality may affect acceptance and performance, but it should not affect temperature-0 correctness. Incorrect draft tokens should be rejected in favor of the target prediction.

Therefore, a draft-only kernel failure does not explain committed token corruption unless there is also a target-verification or alignment bug.

Suspected fault area

The following is a hypothesis, not yet a verified root cause.

Given that:

  1. The accept rule appears to emit only target_predict;
  2. The corruption reproduces at temperature 0;
  3. The corruption disappears at a two-position verify window;
  4. The rate generally increases with verify-window width;
  5. Multiple numerical-determinism interventions had no effect; and
  6. The issue depends on concurrent heterogeneous batching,

the likely fault is in the target verify forward for multi-position DSPARK verification, especially for in-block positions t >= 1.

Potential areas include:

  • Intra-block causal masking
  • Position-ID construction or indexing
  • KV-cache placement for draft positions
  • Request-to-token mapping under heterogeneous batching
  • CUDA graph replay metadata for TARGET_VERIFY
  • Batch-slot reuse or stale per-request metadata
  • dsv4 attention behavior during multi-token verification

The current evidence suggests the target verification pass is computing incorrect logits or associating correct logits with the wrong request/position.

We have not yet isolated the specific kernel or metadata transition.

Suggested next diagnostics

A useful first datapoint would be:

--speculative-dspark-block-size 2

This would help distinguish between:

  • Failure beginning at the first genuinely multi-position verify step; and
  • Error probability accumulating with larger verify windows.

Other useful comparisons may include:

  1. DSPARK with CUDA graphs disabled.
  2. DSPARK with the hierarchical cache disabled.
  3. DSPARK with radix cache and chunked prefill disabled.
  4. An alternate attention backend, if DeepSeek-V4-Flash supports one.
  5. Capturing target_predict before acceptance and comparing it against independent one-token target forwards.
  6. Logging request IDs, verify positions, position IDs, and KV locations for the first divergent token.

Workaround

Both of the following avoid the observed corruption:

Option 1: Disable speculative decoding

This is the safest workaround.

Option 2: Use block_size=1

--speculative-algorithm DSPARK \
--speculative-dspark-block-size 1

This produced zero true typos across:

  • 4,561 grounded identifiers at temperature 0
  • 3,701 grounded identifiers at temperature 1

However, this sacrifices most of the speculative speedup, so it is a mitigation rather than a practical fix.

Until the multi-position verification issue is resolved, DSPARK should not be used with DeepSeek-V4-Flash for workloads where exact token reproduction matters.

Reproduction notes

DeepGEMM JIT warmup

Changing:

--speculative-dspark-block-size

changes num_tokens_per_req and invalidates the DeepGEMM JIT shape cache.

The first launch after changing this value may compile approximately 16,000 shapes and exceed a 3,600-second readiness budget. If the process is killed during warmup, it may look like an unrelated startup failure.

Please allow additional warmup time when changing the block size.

Log probabilities unavailable

DSPARK currently rejects:

"return_logprob": true

with:

DFLASH speculative decoding does not support return_logprob yet

Therefore, per-token target margins cannot currently be collected over HTTP on the affected speculative arm.

Severity

This is a silent data-corruption issue, not only a quality or performance regression.

The generated response is well-formed, and the corrupted identifier often looks plausible. Downstream systems therefore have no reliable way to distinguish the incorrect value from an intended value.

For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, this makes multi-position DSPARK speculative decoding unsafe for exact-identifier and tool-use workloads.

### Reproduction

Reproduction

The corruption usually requires concurrent, heterogeneous batching. A single request in isolation may not reproduce it. The script below sends four byte-identical target requests and four variable-length distractor requests per round.

1. Launch the affected DSPARK configuration

python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <deepseek-v4-flash-0731> \
  --tp 4 \
  --attention-backend dsv4 \
  --moe-runner-backend marlin \
  --speculative-algorithm DSPARK \
  --speculative-dspark-block-size 6 \
  --max-running-requests 16 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 16

2. Save the reproduction script

Save the following code as dspark_typo_repro.py:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Concurrency typo probe for one model and temperature."""

import collections
import concurrent.futures
import json
import os
import re
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request


MODEL = os.environ["TEST_MODEL"]
TEMP = float(os.environ.get("TEST_TEMP", "0"))
ROUNDS = int(os.environ.get("TEST_ROUNDS", "30"))
BASE = os.environ.get("TEST_BASE_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:30000")
URL = f"{BASE}/v1/chat/completions"

IDS = [
    "kimi-k3",
    "nova-x7",
    "atlas-j9",
    "wq-7f2b",
    "zeta-r1",
    "apollo-n9",
]

CTX = " ".join(
    f"event{i}=ok latency={i % 37}ms owner=team{i % 9}"
    for i in range(350)
)

PROMPT = (
    f"Analyze this deployment history and write a 6-section operational report. "
    f"{CTX}\n"
    f"Canonical identifiers: {', '.join(IDS)}. "
    "Include a table and prose recap. "
    "Use every identifier at least four times, always verbatim; "
    "do not invent or normalize identifiers."
)

RX = re.compile(r"[a-z][a-z0-9]*-[a-z0-9]+", re.I)


def lev(a, b):
    prev = list(range(len(b) + 1))

    for i, x in enumerate(a, 1):
        cur = [i]

        for j, y in enumerate(b, 1):
            cur.append(
                min(
                    cur[-1] + 1,
                    prev[j] + 1,
                    prev[j - 1] + (x != y),
                )
            )

        prev = cur

    return prev[-1]


def ask(prompt=PROMPT, max_tokens=700, retries=5):
    body = json.dumps(
        {
            "model": MODEL,
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
            "max_tokens": max_tokens,
            "temperature": TEMP,
            "top_p": 1.0,
        }
    ).encode()

    for n in range(retries):
        request = urllib.request.Request(
            URL,
            data=body,
            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
        )

        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=300) as response:
                result = json.load(response)
                return result["choices"][0]["message"]["content"] or ""
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            if error.code not in (429, 503) or n + 1 == retries:
                raise

            time.sleep(0.3 * (n + 1))

    raise RuntimeError("retries exhausted")


wrong = collections.Counter()
truncations = collections.Counter()
error_types = collections.Counter()

exact = 0
grounded = 0
responses = 0
errors = 0
typo_responses = 0
started = time.time()

with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:

    f"truncations={sum(truncations.values())}"

`gridDim.z` overflow in trtllm-gen sparse MLA (flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3125) is still reachable
from sglang, and still silent. On SM100, any **single unchunked extend of more than 65535 tokens**
on the DSA `prefill=trtllm` path launches **zero** attention kernels, leaves the attention output
tensor **uninitialized**, raises **no** Python exception, and returns garbage. `bench_one_batch`
hits this by construction for `--input-len > 65535`.

The onset is exact: **65535 tokens works, 65536 does not.**

### Relation to existing reports (please read before closing as duplicate)

| prior art | state | why this report is not covered by it |
|---|---|---|
| flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3125 — "trtllm-gen attention error on large batch size" | closed 2026-04-21, **no fix commit** | Correctly diagnosed the root cause. Maintainer proposed "just raise an error"; that was never implemented. `fmhaKernels.cuh` still has a bare `int numCtasZ = params.mBatchSize;` and `cuErrCheck` still only `fprintf`s. |
| sgl-project/sglang#29453 — GLM-5.2 NVFP4 DP4 long-context crash | closed 2026-06-27, **no code fix** | Same root cause, but reported via a *downstream* symptom (invalid sampling probabilities) under **DP attention**, and closed after the reporter worked around it with `--chunked-prefill-size`. No guard landed. |
| sgl-project/sglang#29522 — "Guard Blackwell TRT-LLM prefill chunk size" | **closed, not merged** | The only guard attempt. It capped `chunked_prefill_size` / `get_max_chunk_capacity()` in `server_args.py` + `forward_batch_deepseek_mha_mixin.py` — i.e. **server config only**, gated on `enable_dp_attention`. It would not have covered the direct-ModelRunner path (`bench_one_batch`, `dp_size=1`) at all, and it never landed anyway. |
| flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3238 — `cum_seq_lens_q` for trtllm-gen MLA | merged 2026-06-24 | This is the structural cure (stop flattening tokens into the batch dim), but sglang has **not adopted it**: `dsa_backend.py:3242` still does `q_all.view(batch_size, 1, num_heads, head_dim)`. |

**New in this report:** (a) the fault is reachable with `dp_size=1` on the plain ModelRunner path,
which no proposed guard covered; (b) an exact one-token onset bisection (65535 vs 65536); (c) direct
proof of *silent corruption* — a sentinel-filled `out` tensor comes back untouched — rather than an
inferred downstream symptom; (d) profiler proof that `0` of `num_layers` attention kernels run, so
`bench_one_batch` silently reports **falsely fast** long-context prefill numbers.

Also worth noting: sglang already guards this exact hardware limit elsewhere —
`python/sglang/srt/layers/rotary_embedding/base.py:298` gates a fused kernel on
`query.shape[0] < 65535`, and `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/mamba_slot_fused.py:133` comments
"gridDim.y/z cap at 65535". The DSA attention path has no such check.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA B200 (SM100), driver 590.48.01 |
| sglang | `18107e38d266a98f59a8e3c766f8ddaf9b723ded` (main, 2026-08-14) |
| flashinfer-python | 0.6.17 |
| sglang-kernel | 0.4.6.post1 |
| torch | 2.13.0 / Python 3.12.3 |
| resolved backends | `Set DSA backends for fp8_e4m3 KV Cache: prefill=trtllm, decode=trtllm.` |

`prefill=trtllm` here is the **auto-selected default** for fp8 KV on SM100 — no
`--dsa-prefill-backend` flag was passed. (`enable_auto_select_prefill_impl` at
`dsa_backend.py:350` is only true when the resolved impl is literally `flashmla_auto`, so the
`flashmla_sparse`/`flashmla_kv` rewrite in `set_dsa_prefill_impl` does not apply here.)

Reproduced on two models and two TP degrees: a 78-layer DSA MLA model at TP8, and a 47-layer
`DeepseekV32ForCausalLM` fp8 checkpoint (`index_topk=2048`) at TP2. TP degree is irrelevant — the
overflowing dimension is the token/pseudo-batch dimension, which TP does not shard.

Note `SGLANG_DSA_PREFILL_DENSE_ATTN_KV_LEN_THRESHOLD` defaults to **2048**
(`python/sglang/srt/environ.py:1375`), so both 32768 and 131072 take the same MLA path — the
difference in behaviour is purely the 65535 overflow, not an MHA/MLA path switch.

## Minimal reproducer (no model, no sglang, ~30 s)

Same FlashInfer entry point sglang calls, with a sentinel-filled `out` so "did the kernel run?" is
directly observable:

```python
import sys, torch, flashinfer

B = int(sys.argv[1])                       # pseudo-batch == number of query tokens
NH, TOPK, KVL, ROPE, HD = 16, 2048, 512, 64, 576
PAGE, PAGES, SENT = 64, 8192, -31337.0

kv  = torch.zeros(PAGES, 1, PAGE, HD, dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, device="cuda")
ws  = torch.empty(256 << 20, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
q   = torch.zeros(B, 1, NH, HD, dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, device="cuda")
bt  = torch.zeros(B, 1, TOPK, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
sl  = torch.full((B,), TOPK, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
out = torch.full((B, 1, NH, KVL), SENT, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")

flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(
    query=q, kv_cache=kv, workspace_buffer=ws,
    qk_nope_head_dim=KVL, kv_lora_rank=KVL, qk_rope_head_dim=ROPE,
    block_tables=bt, seq_lens=sl, max_seq_len=TOPK,
    sparse_mla_top_k=TOPK, out=out, bmm1_scale=1.0, backend="trtllm-gen",
)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"B={B} out_untouched={(out == SENT).all().item()}")
```

| pseudo-batch `B` (= `gridDim.z`) | output written? | stderr `CUDA Error` lines | Python exception |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 / 32768 / 65534 | yes | 0 | none |
| **65535** | **yes** | 0 | none |
| **65536** | **NO — 100 % of `out` still holds the sentinel** | 1 | **none** |
| 65537 / 98304 / 131072 | NO | 1 | none |

The only symptom is one stderr line per failed launch:

```
CUDA Error: CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE .../flashinfer/data/include/flashinfer/trtllm/fmha/fmhaKernels.cuh 388
```

## End-to-end reproducer

```bash
python -m sglang.bench_one_batch \
  --model-path <DeepSeek-V3.2-style DSA checkpoint> \
  --tp-size 2 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --disable-cuda-graph \
  --batch-size 1 --input-len 32768 65535 65536 --output-len 8
```

`bench_one_batch` drives the ModelRunner directly, so each `--input-len` is **one unchunked
extend** and `dp_size == 1`.

Result on a 47-layer `DeepseekV32ForCausalLM` fp8 checkpoint at TP2:

| `--input-len` | prefill latency | prefill throughput | swallowed launch errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32768 | 0.710 s | 46 167 tok/s | 0 |
| **65535** | **2.195 s** | 29 853 tok/s | **0** |
| **65536** | **1.222 s** | **53 614 tok/s** | **47 layers x 2 ranks (87 intact stderr lines + 7 mangled by concurrent rank writes)** |

One extra token makes the prefill **1.80x faster** (2.195 s -> 1.222 s), because 44 % of the work
(all of attention) silently disappears. The failure count matches one launch per layer per rank
(concurrent rank writes interleave a few stderr lines), and is precisely zero below the threshold.

**On this model the run did not crash at all** — it completed all 8 decode steps and printed
benchmark numbers. On the 78-layer TP8 model the same condition instead ended in
`torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` at
`model_runner.synchronize()`. So the observable outcome ranges from "wrong answers, no diagnostics"
to "delayed IMA", depending on the model.

Through the HTTP server the same thing happens with `--chunked-prefill-size -1` (documented at
`python/sglang/srt/server_args.py:7225` as "keeps a request in a single forward") or any
`--chunked-prefill-size > 65535`, plus a request longer than 65535 tokens. Auto-selected chunk
sizes (2048-16384 by GPU class) keep default servers below the threshold.

## Observed vs expected

torch-profiler GPU trace, rank 0, 78-layer model, single extend:

| run | attention kernels | attention time | total kernel time |
|---|---|---|---|
| direct runner, extend 32768 | **78** `fmhaSm100fKernel_QkvE4m3O...TokenSparse...` (= `num_layers`) | 425.58 ms | 1192.20 ms |
| direct runner, extend 131072 | **0** — the whole attention bucket is absent | 0 ms | 4079.30 ms |
| HTTP server, 131072 chunked at 16384 | **624** (= 8 chunks x 78 layers) | 1755.94 ms | 5986.66 ms |

Arithmetic check: the correct chunked run spends `5986.66 - 1755.94 = 4230.72 ms` outside
attention; the broken unchunked run's **entire** runtime is 4079.30 ms — 3.6 % apart, leaving no
room for any attention work. So `bench_one_batch` above 64K does not merely crash later, it reports
a prefill that is ~30 % too fast.

Everything *around* attention still runs at 131072 — the sparse indexer
(`deep_gemm::sm100_mqa_logits`), top-k selection (`topk_transform_prefill_kernel`) and the KV write
(`set_mla_kv_buffer_kernel`, 78 launches) are all present. Only the attention kernel is missing, so
nothing upstream signals a problem.

**Expected**: either `num_layers` attention kernels, or a loud failure. Never a normal return with
an unwritten output tensor.

## Root cause

Prefill reuses the *decode* kernel by turning every query token into its own batch entry.

`python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsa_backend.py` @ `18107e38`:
* `:1905` — extend with `dsa_impl == "trtllm" and not self.use_mha` -> `_forward_trtllm(..., is_prefill=True)`
* `:3201` — `transform_index_page_table_prefill(..., output_num_tokens=q.shape[0])` -> one row **per query token**
* `:3230` — `batch_size = page_table_1.shape[0]` -> number of extend tokens
* `:3242` — `q = q_all.view(batch_size, 1, num_heads, head_dim)`
* `:3256` — `flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(..., backend="trtllm-gen")`

flashinfer 0.6.17, `include/flashinfer/trtllm/fmha/fmhaKernels.cuh`:
* `:516` — `int numCtasZ = params.mBatchSize;`
* `:640` — `ctaLaunchParams.mNumCtasZ = numCtasZ;`
* `:413` — `launch_config.gridDimZ = ctaLaunchParams.mNumCtasZ;`
* `:388` — `cuErrCheck(cuLaunchKernelEx(&launch_config, func, kernelParamsList, nullptr));`

CUDA's maximum `gridDim.z` is 65535, so `batch_size >= 65536` makes `cuLaunchKernelEx` return
`CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE`. That return value is then discarded —
`include/flashinfer/trtllm/common.h`:

```cpp
:44  inline void cuErrCheck_(CUresult stat, char const* file, int line) {
:45    if (stat != CUDA_SUCCESS) {
:46      char const* msg = nullptr;
:47      cuGetErrorName(stat, &msg);
:48      fprintf(stderr, "CUDA Error: %s %s %d\n", msg, file, line);   // prints, then returns
:49    }
:50  }
```

A launch-configuration error is also **not** a sticky context error, so nothing downstream notices
either — until corrupted values eventually produce an out-of-range index and the IMA.

## Suggested fixes

1. **sglang, smallest useful change**: in `_forward_trtllm`'s `is_prefill` branch, split the call
   into `ceil(batch_size / 65535)` launches, or at minimum `raise` when `batch_size > 65535` so the
   failure is loud. This is the only fix that also protects `bench_one_batch` / `dp_size=1`.
2. **sglang, structural**: adopt `cum_seq_lens_q` (flashinfer#3238, merged) so prefill stops
   flattening tokens into the batch dimension.
3. **FlashInfer**: implement what was agreed in #3125 — `FLASHINFER_CHECK(numCtasZ <= 65535, ...)`,
   and make `cuErrCheck` raise rather than `fprintf`, so no trtllm-gen launch failure can ever be
   silent again.

Two minimal fail-loud PRs accompany this issue: an sglang-side guard implementing the `raise` from
(1), and a FlashInfer-side pre-launch check implementing (3)'s `FLASHINFER_CHECK` (links in the
first comment below). The chunk-split from (1) and the `cum_seq_lens_q` adoption (2) remain open as
the actual capability fix.

## Note on the test environment

The FlashInfer install carries one local, build-only deviation from the 0.6.17 release: in
`fmhaKernels.cuh`, three `#if CUDA_VERSION >= 13030` guards (lines 134/150/167) were extended with
`&& defined(FLASHINFER_ENABLE_RUBIN_OVERSIZED_SMEM)` so the file compiles against a CUDA header set
lacking `CU_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_SHARED_MEMORY_MODE`. Those blocks only handle SM107 (Rubin) oversized
shared memory and are dead code on SM100; they cannot affect grid configuration.

(all of attention) silently disappears. The error count is exactly `num_layers x tp_size`: one
failed launch per layer per rank, and precisely zero below the threshold.

**On this model the run did not crash at all** — it completed all 8 decode steps and printed
benchmark numbers. On the 78-layer TP8 model the same condition instead ended in
`torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` at
`model_runner.synchronize()`. So the observable outcome ranges from "wrong answers, no diagnostics"
to "delayed IMA", depending on the model.

Through the HTTP server the same thing happens with `--chunked-prefill-size -1` (documented at
`python/sglang/srt/server_args.py:7225` as "keeps a request in a single forward") or any
`--chunked-prefill-size > 65535`, plus a request longer than 65535 tokens. Auto-selected chunk
sizes (2048-16384 by GPU class) keep default servers below the threshold.

## Observed vs expected

torch-profiler GPU trace, rank 0, 78-layer model, single extend:

| run | attention kernels | attention time | total kernel time |
|---|---|---|---|
| direct runner, extend 32768 | **78** `fmhaSm100fKernel_QkvE4m3O...TokenSparse...` (= `num_layers`) | 425.58 ms | 1192.20 ms |
| direct runner, extend 131072 | **0** — the whole attention bucket is absent | 0 ms | 4079.30 ms |
| HTTP server, 131072 chunked at 16384 | **624** (= 8 chunks x 78 layers) | 1755.94 ms | 5986.66 ms |

Arithmetic check: the correct chunked run spends `5986.66 - 1755.94 = 4230.72 ms` outside
attention; the broken unchunked run's **entire** runtime is 4079.30 ms — 3.6 % apart, leaving no
room for any attention work. So `bench_one_batch` above 64K does not merely crash later, it reports
a prefill that is ~30 % too fast.

Everything *around* attention still runs at 131072 — the sparse indexer
(`deep_gemm::sm100_mqa_logits`), top-k selection (`topk_transform_prefill_kernel`) and the KV write
(`set_mla_kv_buffer_kernel`, 78 launches) are all present. Only the attention kernel is missing, so
nothing upstream signals a problem.

**Expected**: either `num_layers` attention kernels, or a loud failure. Never a normal return with
an unwritten output tensor.

## Root cause

Prefill reuses the *decode* kernel by turning every query token into its own batch entry.

`python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsa_backend.py` @ `18107e38`:
* `:1905` — extend with `dsa_impl == "trtllm" and not self.use_mha` -> `_forward_trtllm(..., is_prefill=True)`
* `:3201` — `transform_index_page_table_prefill(..., output_num_tokens=q.shape[0])` -> one row **per query token**
* `:3230` — `batch_size = page_table_1.shape[0]` -> number of extend tokens
* `:3242` — `q = q_all.view(batch_size, 1, num_heads, head_dim)`
* `:3256` — `flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(..., backend="trtllm-gen")`

flashinfer 0.6.17, `include/flashinfer/trtllm/fmha/fmhaKernels.cuh`:
* `:516` — `int numCtasZ = params.mBatchSize;`
* `:640` — `ctaLaunchParams.mNumCtasZ = numCtasZ;`
* `:413` — `launch_config.gridDimZ = ctaLaunchParams.mNumCtasZ;`
* `:388` — `cuErrCheck(cuLaunchKernelEx(&launch_config, func, kernelParamsList, nullptr));`

CUDA's maximum `gridDim.z` is 65535, so `batch_size >= 65536` makes `cuLaunchKernelEx` return
`CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE`. That return value is then discarded —
`include/flashinfer/trtllm/common.h`:

```cpp
:44  inline void cuErrCheck_(CUresult stat, char const* file, int line) {
:45    if (stat != CUDA_SUCCESS) {
:46      char const* msg = nullptr;
:47      cuGetErrorName(stat, &msg);
:48      fprintf(stderr, "CUDA Error: %s %s %d\n", msg, file, line);   // prints, then returns
:49    }
:50  }
```

A launch-configuration error is also **not** a sticky context error, so nothing downstream notices
either — until corrupted values eventually produce an out-of-range index and the IMA.

## Suggested fixes

1. **sglang, smallest useful change**: in `_forward_trtllm`'s `is_prefill` branch, split the call
   into `ceil(batch_size / 65535)` launches, or at minimum `raise` when `batch_size > 65535` so the
   failure is loud. This is the only fix that also protects `bench_one_batch` / `dp_size=1`.
2. **sglang, structural**: adopt `cum_seq_lens_q` (flashinfer#3238, merged) so prefill stops
   flattening tokens into the batch dimension.
3. **FlashInfer**: implement what was agreed in #3125 — `FLASHINFER_CHECK(numCtasZ <= 65535, ...)`,
   and make `cuErrCheck` raise rather than `fprintf`, so no trtllm-gen launch failure can ever be
   silent again.

Happy to send the sglang-side PR (1) and a companion FlashInfer PR (3) if maintainers agree on the
preferred shape.

## Note on the test environment

The FlashInfer install carries one local, build-only deviation from the 0.6.17 release: in
`fmhaKernels.cuh`, three `#if CUDA_VERSION >= 13030` guards (lines 134/150/167) were extended with
`&& defined(FLASHINFER_ENABLE_RUBIN_OVERSIZED_SMEM)` so the file compiles against a CUDA header set
lacking `CU_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_SHARED_MEMORY_MODE`. Those blocks only handle SM107 (Rubin) oversized
shared memory and are dead code on SM100; they cannot affect grid configuration.

items.title: [Feature] Bit-exact correctness coverage for Unified Radix Cache
items.body:
## Motivation

Cache correctness is difficult to verify from model output alone. A corrupted KV block or recurrent-state checkpoint can still produce fluent text, and the resulting numerical drift can remain far below the tolerance used by accuracy and KL tests. These failures have shipped because the existing signals are approximate.

Bit-exact logprob consistency turns one of these approximate signals into a correctness oracle. `kl_test_utils` evaluates the same token through prefill and decode. If both paths are batch-invariant and compute the same function, they must produce identical logprobs. Once that baseline is established, the contract for every cache-reuse path becomes:

> **Any nonzero KL is a KV/state reuse bug.**

This is stronger than threshold-based testing. It does not ask whether the error is large enough to matter to a benchmark. It asks whether restoring cached state is exactly equivalent to recomputing it. Bugs that previously sat below a model-specific noise floor become unambiguous regressions.

Examples:

- Incorrect reused state: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34043, https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34184, https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29792

## Foundation

Bit-exactness depends on the model and execution path. Deterministic inference can remove batch-dependent kernel and communication behavior, but it cannot make two mathematically different algorithms identical. For example, Qwen3-Next uses different GDN kernels for prefill and decode, and retains a nonzero numerical floor.

Inkling provides the combination needed for continuous gating. Its prefill and decode paths compute the same function, so under deterministic inference its prefill-versus-decode KL is exactly `0`. A shrunken checkpoint runs on one GPU. The model also contains `FULL`, `SWA`, and `MAMBA` cache components, so one test process exercises full KV, sliding-window, and recurrent-state reuse together.

The resulting foundation has four layers:

1. deterministic execution makes repeated computation batch-invariant;
2. logprob consistency establishes an exact prefill/decode baseline;
3. cache tests apply that baseline to each state restoration path;
4. revert-then-red validation proves that each regression guard can detect the defect it claims to cover.

Supporting work:

- Inkling deterministic execution: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33417, https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34159
- Workflow tools: [KL consistency test skill](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/tree/main/.claude/skills/kl-consistency-test), https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34169
- Real-weight consistency coverage: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34168, https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34356
- Per-commit guards: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34607
- Calibration and follow-up validation: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34405, https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34653

## Roadmap

The remaining work is coverage, not a new testing method. Every feature that can save, move, or restore model state introduces a distinct correctness boundary and needs its own exact-KL test class.

- [x] Base cache path
- [x] Mamba `extra_buffer`
- [x] Mamba `extra_buffer_lazy`
- [x] HiCache multi-turn
- [ ] Speculative decoding
     - [x] MTP
     - [ ] DSpark / DFlash @alphabetc1 
          - Support return_logprob https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35058
- [ ] Unified memory

items.title: PP8 disaggregated prefill has a load-independent ~30 s TTFT floor on Kimi-K3
items.body:
# Describe the issue

A PD-disaggregated Kimi-K3 deployment exhibits a large, load-independent TTFT floor when the prefill node uses pipeline parallelism.

Our PP8 configuration was based on the topology and guidance in the LMSYS post [SGLang and Miles Add Day-0 Support for Kimi K3](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-07-27-kimi-k3-day0-support). The post reports that, for 8K prefill on 2×4 GB300 GPUs, PP8×TP1 reaches 1.45–1.72× the prefill capacity of TEP8 and has lower TTFT after the low-concurrency crossover. However, it does not provide the absolute TTFT values or the detailed TTFT measurement methodology. We are trying to determine whether the behavior below comes from a difference in workload or configuration, or from an unexpected PP control-path latency.

With the prefill node configured as `pp_size=8, tp_size=1`, TTFT p50 is **31.1 s**. On the same two nodes, with the same replay workload and closed-loop concurrency, a `tp_size=8` prefill baseline has a TTFT p50 of **2.33 s**. The PP8 result is therefore about **13.4x slower**.

This does not look like capacity saturation. During the PP8 run:

- Prefill uncached throughput was only 1.1–1.6 K tok/s.
- The prefill waiting queue was only 1–12 requests across all eight PP ranks.
- The decode node had only 1–4 running requests.
- TTFT p50 nevertheless remained between 30 and 33 s for the entire run.

## Expected behavior

At low load, `pp_size=8` on the disaggregated prefill node should not add a load-independent ~30 s TTFT floor. We expect PP to improve or preserve prefill capacity without making latency-sensitive online traffic more than an order of magnitude slower than TP8.

## Actual behavior

The PP8 configuration spends most of TTFT inside the prefill node:

| Prefill stage, median / p90 | TP8 | PP8 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `bootstrap_duration` | 9 ms / 69 ms | **12.45 s / 14.1 s** |
| `queue_duration` | 33 ms / 1.1 s | 1.2 s / 1.8 s |
| `forward_duration` | 1.37 s / 2.4 s | **24.8 s / 27.9 s** |
| `transfer_speed` (bytes divided by first-to-last send span) | 4.0 GB/s | 0.02 GB/s |

On the decode node, bootstrap is about 6 ms and allocation wait is about 3 ms in both configurations. Decode-side `transfer_duration` is 26–34 s with PP8, but that metric includes prefill queueing, forward, and KV transfer. The Mooncake handshake itself is not taking tens of seconds.

## Questions

1. The LMSYS Kimi-K3 post states that PP8×TP1 has lower TTFT in its 8K prefill benchmark, but does not report absolute TTFT values. Could you share the PP8×TP1 and TEP8 TTFT results at the tested concurrency levels, especially around the c1–c4 crossover and in the saturated region? If possible, could you also provide relevant setup details, including chunk size, cache state, and whether the test used standalone or PD-disaggregated prefill? This would help us determine whether our ~30 s floor reflects different benchmark conditions or unexpected behavior.
2. Is a load-independent ~30 s TTFT floor expected for `pp_size=8` with `disaggregation-mode prefill`? At only 1.1–1.6 K uncached tok/s and 1–12 queued requests, we still observe a 12.45 s median bootstrap duration and a 31.1 s median TTFT. If this is not expected, which part of the configuration or runtime should we investigate?
3. Our reading of `event_loop_pp_disagg_prefill` is that bootstrap readiness must traverse all PP ranks and return to rank 0 before the request can be admitted. Is this interpretation correct? Is there a supported or planned way to move this consensus off the PP microbatch critical path? Is the release-consensus traversal only required for Prefill-side resource reclamation, or can it also delay Decode admission and the first token?
4. Our workload has a 94.1% prefix-cache hit rate, so the median uncached tail is only about 3K tokens, smaller than `--chunked-prefill-size 16384`. Is PP8 expected to provide a TTFT benefit only when the uncached input spans multiple chunks? For latency-sensitive, high-prefix-hit traffic, should we use a smaller chunk, dynamic chunking, or TP8 instead?

## Measurements

Both runs use real multi-turn chat sessions, streaming responses, and a closed loop of 20 concurrent sessions.

| Metric | PP8 prefill: `pp_size=8, tp_size=1` | TP8 prefill baseline: `tp_size=8` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Requests | 5,942 | 64,114 |
| **TTFT p50** | **31.1 s** | **2.33 s** |
| TTFT p90 / p99 | 40.5 s / 58.0 s | 4.41 s / 7.73 s |
| TTFT mean | 35.6 s | 2.54 s |
| E2E latency p99 | 94 s | 59 s |
| Inter-token latency mean / p99 | 20 ms / 168 ms | 17 ms / 197 ms |
| Achieved request rate | 0.47 req/s | 2.26 req/s |
| Prefill prompt throughput | 23.1 K tok/s | 139.4 K tok/s |
| Prefill uncached throughput | 1.1–1.6 K tok/s | 5.1–7.3 K tok/s |
| Prefill waiting queue | 1–12 requests | 0–6 requests |
| Decode running requests | 1–4 | 10–18 |
| Prefix cache hit rate | 94.1% | 95.5% |

TTFT p50 sampled every 30 minutes throughout the PP8 run was:

`30.09 / 30.71 / 30.12 / 30.95 / 30.57 / 33.43 / 30.93 / 32.01` seconds.

The workload lengths were:

| Token distribution | PP8 | TP8 baseline |
|---|---:|---:|
| Input p50 / mean | 47,209 / 49,064 | 56,903 / 61,761 |
| Input p90 / p99 | 78,658 / 145,523 | 106,375 / 190,638 |
| Output p50 / mean | 190 / 318 | 208 / 354 |

The TP8 baseline had longer inputs, so the input-length difference does not explain why PP8 has higher TTFT.

### Replay workload and measurement scope

The source workload contains 2,000 multi-turn session traces, comprising 9,562 user turns and approximately 89,992 request records. Both configurations replayed the same source corpus in randomized, interleaved session mode: each selected session advances by one user turn and is then returned to the session pool. Session affinity was enabled, with a closed loop of 20 active sessions.

The measurements are based on stable server-side observation windows rather than one complete pass over an identical number of requests. The PP8 window contains 5,942 engine-observed requests, while the TP8 window contains 64,114. The different request counts result from different observation durations and achieved request rates, not from different source datasets.

## Suspected code path

In SGLang `v0.5.17`, `event_loop_pp_disagg_prefill` in `srt/managers/scheduler_pp_mixin.py` appears to serialize bootstrap admission and KV release confirmation onto the PP microbatch ring.

### Bootstrap admission

With TP, `pop_bootstrapped` is polled directly by the event loop. With PP, the ready request IDs pass through a consensus ring:

1. Rank 0 obtains locally ready request IDs through `_pp_pd_get_bootstrapped_ids`.
2. The list advances by one PP stage per microbatch iteration while ranks intersect their ready sets.
3. The last rank returns the result using `_pp_pd_send_consensus_bootstrapped_ids` and the slot offset `next_first_rank_mb_id = (mb_id + pp_size) % pp_loop_size`.
4. Only after the result returns to rank 0 does `process_bootstrapped_queue` call `pop_bootstrapped(pp_good_rids=...)` and `finalize_bootstrap`.

For `pp_size=8`, this is approximately eight iterations to reach the last rank plus eight iterations to return. With a measured iteration period of about 0.7–1 s under load, the expected wall time is 11–16 s, matching the observed 12.45 s median `bootstrap_duration`.

### KV release confirmation

`completion_time` is set in `process_disagg_prefill_inflight_queue` only after a second consensus path using `_pp_pd_get_prefill_transferred_ids` and `_pp_pd_send_consensus_release_ids`. This appears to add another full PP-ring traversal before the metadata buffer can be reclaimed.

### KV egress

Each PP rank sends its layer slice after that stage completes. The decode node uses DCP8, so the pages are also scattered across eight DCP ranks. The resulting first-to-last transfer span is long even when the inter-node link is not saturated.

The compute side of PP itself is working: in a saturated synthetic benchmark, PP8 rank 0 reports 38–49 K tok/s instantaneous input throughput, 1.9–2.4x the TP8 steady-state rate. However, about 45% of wall time is spent in stalls of at least 2 s, with a cadence consistent with the consensus-ring delay. Average pure-prefill throughput is therefore only 22.5 K tok/s, about 1.10x the 20.4 K tok/s TP8 baseline.

## Configuration differences in the A/B comparison

The aggregate A/B comparison is not perfectly controlled:

- PP8 uses SGLang `v0.5.17`; the TP8 baseline uses `v0.5.16`.
- The TP8 baseline enables FP8 KV cache and DSPARK speculative decoding.
- The PP8 decode node uses DCP8; the TP8 baseline does not use DCP.

We therefore do not rely on the aggregate TTFT difference alone. The PP hypothesis is based primarily on the load-independent 30–33 s floor, the per-request timing breakdown, and the PP event-loop behavior described above.

## What we already tried

- Backported PR #27010 for `PP + hicache L3` control-queue consistency. All eight PP ranks agreed on revoke decisions and correctness checks passed, but TTFT did not improve.
- Changed Mamba state storage to `--mamba-track-interval 1024 --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16`, reducing L3 write amplification from about 59 to 21 KB/token. TTFT did not improve.
- Removed `--disable-custom-all-reduce` on the TP8 baseline, enabling the fused Kimi-K3 all-reduce. Prefill throughput improved by about 9%, but this is not applicable to PP8×TP1 because it has no TP all-reduce.
- Reverted the prefill node to `tp_size=8`. TTFT returned to about 2.3 s.

# Reproduction

## Topology

- Two compute nodes: one prefill node and one decode node.
- Eight NVIDIA B300 GPUs per node.
- Mooncake is used for PD KV transfer.
- The prefill node uses hicache L2 in host DRAM and L3 in Mooncake.
- The decode node does not use hicache.

## Prefill node: PP8×TP1

  --stream-response-default-include-usage
```

## Router

```bash
python3 -m sglang_router.launch_router \
  --pd-disaggregation \
  --prefill http://<PREFILL_NODE>:30000 <BOOTSTRAP_PORT> \
  --decode http://<DECODE_NODE>:30000 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --prefill-policy cache_aware \
  --decode-policy round_robin \
  --balance-abs-threshold 2 \
  --balance-rel-threshold 1.1
```

## Public synthetic benchmark

The following command reproduces the high PP8 TTFT and low average throughput without the private replay dataset:

```bash
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
export TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1

python3 -m sglang.bench_serving \
  --backend sglang \
  --host <ROUTER_HOST> \
  --port 8000 \
  --model <KIMI_K3_MODEL_PATH> \
  --dataset-name random-ids \
  --random-input-len 8192 \
  --random-output-len 1024 \
  --random-range-ratio 1.0 \
  --num-prompts 320 \
  --max-concurrency 64 \
  --flush-cache
```

Observed with PP8: 320/320 requests completed, TTFT p50 14.3 s, TTFT p99 33.8 s, E2E p50 44.0 s, and input throughput 10.8 K tok/s. Decode-side speculative decoding was disabled in this run, so E2E latency is not directly comparable with the TP8 online baseline.

For pure prefill isolation, set output length to one token:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.bench_serving \
  --backend sglang \
  --host <ROUTER_HOST> \
  --port 8000 \
  --model <KIMI_K3_MODEL_PATH> \
  --dataset-name random-ids \
  --random-input-len 8192 \
  --random-output-len 1 \
  --random-range-ratio 1.0 \
  --num-prompts 320 \
  --max-concurrency 64 \
  --flush-cache
```

Observed PP8 pure-prefill input throughput was 22.5 K tok/s, compared with 20.4 K tok/s for the TP8 baseline.

# Environment

## Hardware and deployment specifications

The following output is from the SGLang `v0.5.17-cu130` prefill container used for the PP8 run:
